title: CV Linter distribution options: agent skills, plugins, MCP, and PWA

options.option: Hermes Agent skill with bundled deterministic scripts
pros: Portable skill format: a directory with SKILL.md plus optional scripts, references, and assets; Hermes states compatibility with the open Agent Skills standard.
Invocation is convenient: users can invoke an installed skill explicitly as /cv-linter, and Hermes can also select it from its description; multiple skills can be stacked in one command.
Hermes supports local skill directories, profile isolation, optional skill installation, and skill distribution through its hub or an HTTPS SKILL.md URL.
A CV parser and rule engine can run locally as bundled scripts, avoiding upload of the CV or job description.
Inference: this is the best native UX for a Hermes-first product because it combines a discoverable slash command with local executable logic.
cons: A skill is primarily instructions plus scripts, not a strongly typed capability boundary. File access and command execution remain dependent on the host agent's permissions.
Hermes skills can be modified or deleted by the agent, so a production distribution should protect or verify the installed package if tamper evidence matters.
LLM selection can be implicit unless the skill explicitly requires a separate confirmation step; this is unsuitable for a silent or unrecorded LLM-as-judge default.
Hermes skill metadata is not, by itself, a complete dependency-locking or supply-chain mechanism; the package should add checksums, a manifest, and pinned parser/model versions.

options.option: Claude Code skill or Claude Code plugin
pros: Claude Code supports the same general SKILL.md format and progressive disclosure model, making a core CV Linter skill potentially reusable across compatible agents.
A standalone skill is suitable for personal or project-local workflows; a plugin is explicitly intended for sharing, reusable distribution, and versioned releases.
Claude Code plugins can package skills together with agents, hooks, and MCP servers, allowing a CV Linter plugin to include deterministic helpers and a typed tool interface.
Claude Code provides explicit permission controls for file reads, shell commands, edits, web access, and MCP servers, which supports a least-privilege integration.
Inference: the plugin form is more appropriate than a bare skill when CV Linter needs a stable namespace, release metadata, optional hooks, or an MCP server.
cons: The plugin's namespace changes invocation UX: users invoke names such as /cv-linter-plugin:check rather than a short global command.
Claude Code permissions govern the host integration, but the SKILL.md itself does not create a cryptographic or OS-level privacy boundary.
Claude can automatically invoke some skills when relevant, so the skill must explicitly state that LLM judging is opt-in and must not be inferred from a normal deterministic check.
Claude Code is tied to Claude Code's permission model and plugin manager, so this is not a universal distribution format by itself.

options.option: Codex skill, optionally distributed through a Codex plugin
pros: Codex skills package SKILL.md instructions, optional scripts, references, and assets, and build on the open Agent Skills standard.
Codex supports both explicit invocation through /skills or $skill mentions and implicit activation from the skill description.
Codex uses progressive disclosure and limits the initial skill-description budget, which helps keep a CV-specific workflow from consuming excessive context.
Codex's sandbox and approval model can limit reads, writes, network access, and execution; read-only mode is suitable for deterministic linting.
OpenAI's plugin documentation describes skills as the workflow layer around MCP tools, making a Codex plugin a plausible package for a deterministic local engine plus optional model judging.
Inference: Codex is a strong secondary target if the core package remains Agent Skills-compatible and the deterministic engine is callable without trusting model-generated shell commands.
cons: Codex's implicit activation means a normal request could trigger the skill unless the description and instructions impose an explicit judge-consent gate.
Scripts may require separate approval depending on sandbox and approval configuration, which can add friction to first use.
Codex's filesystem boundary is configured by the host and workspace; the skill cannot guarantee privacy independently of those settings.
Codex plugin packaging is newer and more host-specific than the base Agent Skills directory format, so a plugin-only release would reduce portability.
Inference: deterministic checks should be exposed as a bounded executable or MCP tool rather than asking Codex to reproduce parsing logic through free-form commands.

options.option: Local or remote MCP server exposing CV Linter tools
pros: MCP provides a standardized tool interface for live capabilities, and can also expose resources and prompts; this maps naturally to parse_cv, lint_cv, compare_to_job, and judge_cv operations.
A local stdio MCP server can keep parsing and deterministic checks on the user's machine, while a separately configured remote model provider can be optional.

Tool schemas make inputs and outputs more auditable than a prompt-only skill: the server can require explicit fields such as cv_path, job_description, ruleset_version, judge_enabled, model_id, and consent_token.
MCP clients are expected to validate inputs and outputs, request confirmation for sensitive operations, show tool inputs, apply timeouts, and log tool usage.
Hermes supports local stdio and remote HTTP MCP servers, automatic discovery, per-server filtering, and MCP resources/prompts.
cons: MCP itself does not guarantee privacy: a remote server can receive CV content, and even a local server may be given overly broad filesystem access by its client configuration.
Installation and configuration are more complex than installing a skill, especially for users who only want an interactive CV review.
A prompt exposed through MCP can still be manipulated by untrusted document content; the server must treat CV and job-description text as data, not instructions.
MCP tool approval and logging behavior depends partly on the client, so CV Linter should maintain its own structured audit record rather than relying only on client logs.
Inference: MCP should be the execution boundary for deterministic operations and optional judging, while the Agent Skill should supply the human-facing workflow and explanation.

options.option: Standalone browser application or installable PWA
pros: A browser/PWA has a familiar drag-and-drop workflow and does not require users to install an agent, skill manager, or MCP client.
Browser file selection provides a naturally narrow boundary: the app receives files the user explicitly selects rather than arbitrary paths on disk.
A PWA can cache application resources with a service worker and support offline deterministic checks when its parser and rules engine are shipped locally.
The File System API and origin-private file system can support local processing and local result storage without granting unrestricted native filesystem access.
Inference: the PWA is the strongest fallback for non-agent users and the best visual report surface, but not the best sole distribution mechanism for agent workflows.
cons: Browser file-system capabilities vary by browser and platform; PWA file handlers are currently limited in important ways, including Chromium-oriented support.
A hosted PWA can silently make network requests unless the application clearly surfaces network state and provides an offline-only mode.
A browser sandbox cannot itself run every native parser or local model; WebAssembly or client-side model packaging may increase download size and implementation complexity.
Agent invocation is indirect: an agent generally cannot inspect a user's selected file or PWA state without an explicit bridge such as upload, local API, or MCP server.
Browser storage can be evicted or cleared, so audit records should be exportable and should not rely solely on local browser storage.
Inference: the PWA should consume the same versioned lint-result schema as the agent integrations rather than becoming a separate rules implementation.

recommendation: Use a layered distribution architecture: (1) publish a versioned, Agent Skills-compatible core package containing SKILL.md, deterministic parser/linter scripts, rule definitions, schemas, fixtures, and an explicit privacy policy; (2) expose the deterministic engine through a small local executable and optionally a local stdio MCP server with narrowly scoped operations; (3) ship thin adapters for Hermes, Claude Code, and Codex, using each host's native skill/plugin packaging but keeping the core logic identical; and (4) retain the PWA as a visual, drag-and-drop client over the same engine and result schema. Make `lint` the default and strictly deterministic: parse only user-selected paths or content, never recursively scan home directories, never make network requests, and return rule IDs, evidence spans, ruleset version, parser version, input hashes, and warnings. Make `judge` a separate explicit operation or flag, disabled by default. Before judging, show a consent summary naming the model/provider, whether CV text leaves the device, fields that will be sent, estimated cost if available, and retention/training implications. Support local models as the privacy-preserving judge option and remote models only through opt-in provider configuration. Record an append-only audit object for every judge run containing consent timestamp, model/provider identifier, model and prompt-template versions, ruleset/parser versions, input and output hashes, redaction policy, findings, and uncertainty. Do not allow the LLM judge to override deterministic failures; label its output as advisory, include evidence excerpts and rubric scores, and require structured JSON validation. Version the package with SemVer, pin parser/ruleset/prompt-template versions independently, embed a manifest and checksums, publish signed release artifacts, and make reports reproducible by recording all version identifiers. This recommendation is an architectural inference based on the cited capabilities and limitations, not a stated requirement of any one platform.
privacy_notes: Default data path should be local: user-selected file or pasted text goes to the local parser, deterministic rule engine, and local report generator without network access.

Treat file access as an allowlist, not a capability inferred from the current working directory. Accept explicit paths or bytes, reject traversal and symlink escapes where applicable, and do not scan unrelated directories.
Separate deterministic linting from LLM judging at the API, UI, and audit-log levels. A request to lint must never implicitly upload the CV or invoke a model.
When remote judging is enabled, send the minimum necessary content, preferably redacted or chunked, and disclose the exact provider endpoint and model identifier before transmission.
Treat CVs, job descriptions, and extracted document metadata as untrusted data. Prompt-injection text inside a document must not alter tool permissions, network policy, rubric, or audit behavior.
MCP clients should be configured with a local stdio server and narrowly scoped paths; remote MCP should be considered data egress and require separate consent.

Agent hosts provide different permission guarantees. Hermes skills rely heavily on host permissions, Claude Code and Codex provide approval/sandbox controls, and a PWA provides browser-origin isolation; CV Linter should enforce its own validation and audit layer across all adapters.
Persist hashes and structured findings by default rather than raw CV text. Offer an explicit export containing the original text only when the user requests it.
A report should distinguish deterministic findings, LLM-advisory findings, and unresolved or low-confidence findings. Never present an LLM score as an objective lint result.
Use pinned versions for rules, parser, prompt template, judge model, and adapter package. Include these identifiers in every report so a later rerun can explain differences.
